captions.text: Bee hears everything I learn: lectures, study sessions, podcasts.
It can summarize them and remember them for me.
But in an interview, I'm the one who has to know it.
Practicing recall is one of the best-tested ways to learn.
Recall turns what Bee heard into quizzes on my wrist that I answer out loud.
Bee's transcript is the answer sheet.

beats.name: How it works
needs_operator: MISSING: the answer page for 'What two types of glass are needed in a fiber optic cable and why?' is not in E (the question appears only as a row in Today's answers). 12 s slot is a slate; the final render is blocked until it exists
A/B sync offset estimated from DB alarm times, +-2 s
B footage is dimmed; brightened x1.65 in post

captions.text: When a learning session ends, Recall pulls the transcript through the Bee CLI
and skips anything casual or personal.
Claude Haiku on Amazon Bedrock writes the questions, each tied to the moment I heard it.
When I'm free, I say so, or tick a todo. Each question goes out as a Bee todo with an alarm.
Recall reads Bee's live transcript while I'm talking, grades me against a rubric,
and sends feedback the same way. Spaced repetition decides when I see it again.

beats.name: Why waits

scenes.text: Recall: 6 questions are buzzing for you. Say Hey Bee, let's do a Recall session when you can talk.

needs_operator: Nudge N shown as 6; stings.py fills in the real due count

captions.text: My first version quizzed me at random times.
Six prompts, four missed: driving, asleep, or the alert hit my phone. So Recall waits for you.
It nudges after a lecture and in your active hours, holds off while Bee hears you talking,
and a missed question never counts against you.
